name: Find water
summary: Work outward from the closest, least exposed water; that is a rough order, not a safety grade. Sealed bottled water is ready to drink. Next is water already inside buildings: a tank water heater, the pipes, office water coolers, ice in freezers and, as a last resort, a toilet tank (not the bowl) with clear water and no cleaner in it. Then rain off roofs and tarps when it isn't freezing, and snow and ice when it is. Then springs and wells, which need less treatment than lakes and rivers but stop when an electric pump loses power. Lakes, rivers and ponds come last, and in winter they are under ice. Treat all of it except sealed bottled water: clear it first, then boil or disinfect. Some water can't be made safe at home: heating systems and boilers, anything that smells of fuel or chemicals, and lakes or ponds with an algae bloom.

parts.why: Water already in heaters, pipes, toilet tanks and coolers
Jugs, pails and drums to carry and hold water
Plain unscented bleach to disinfect clear water; not pool or hot-tub chemicals, which carry other additives
Clears and cleans water from outdoor sources
Siphons water out of tanks, cisterns and heaters; use a hose made for drinking water
Lowers a bucket into a well or an ice hole
Hand and 12 V pumps for wells and tanks
Catches rain where there is no roof

tips: Tank water heater: turn off its power or gas, drain it from its drain valve into a clean container, and don't switch it back on while it's empty (Washington DOH, FEMA 2004). Use the tank that feeds your taps, not a heating system's (CDC find water).

Pipes: shut the main valve so contaminated water can't flow in, open a tap on the top floor, then draw from the lowest tap (Washington DOH, FEMA 2004). A garden hose not made for drinking water can add lead or chemicals (Cleveland Water hose).

A toilet tank (not the bowl) is a last resort, only if the water is clear and no cleaner or tablet has been in it (CDC find water, MSU Extension, FEMA 2004); Washington DOH says not to use it. Pool and hot-tub water is for washing, cleaning and flushing only, never drinking (CDC find water).
Never drink from boilers, radiators or a hot-water heating system (CDC), or from waterbeds (Washington DOH). Boiling and bleach can't fix water with fuel or chemicals in it (CDC).

Outdoors, take flowing water over still, and skip floating material, a dark colour or a strange smell (EPA). Springs and groundwater need less treatment than lakes and rivers (Sphere), but all outside water needs treating (CDC find water); boiling beats bleach against Cryptosporidium (CDC).

If a flood reached a well, disinfect and test it before use (EPA). Switch off the pump's power before you work at the well, and don't go down into a well pit or pump house: gas builds up there (CDC well disinfection). Treat a well or cistern the same way; bad air kills rescuers too.

Melt snow before you drink it: eating snow lowers your core temperature (TC 21-3). Skip snow cleared from roads and parking lots, which can hold salt, oil and heavy metals (TAC snow). A stream or a hole in lake ice saves the fuel that melting takes.
Cover an ice hole to slow refreezing (TC 21-3), and mark it with a large branch so nobody steps in it. Never go on the ice alone (Cottage Life). Read the ice guide before you go out.
Avoid algae blooms in any season. Boiling doesn't remove their toxins and can concentrate them, and blooms can grow under snow and ice (HealthLinkBC 47).

Treat everything except sealed bottled water: settle or filter it, then boil it at least 1 minute, or add plain unscented bleach, never pool or hot-tub chemicals (EPA, Health Canada well treatment). Water under 10 °C needs double the bleach and 1 to 2 hours (HealthLinkBC 49b).
